INTRODUCTION\n1. This Performance and Learning Review (PLR) assesses the implementation of the World Bank\nGroup FY20-25 Country Partnership Framework (CPF) for the United Mexican States.1 The CPF was\ndiscussed by the Board on February 27, 2020, at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Covering six years, it\naims to support three interlinked goals: (a) more rapid, more inclusive growth; (b) stronger institutions for\npublic finance, service delivery, and economic inclusion; and (c) sustainable infrastructure and climate action.\n2. The objectives of this PLR are to assess progress in CPF implementation and propose adjustments\nfor the remainder of the CPF period. The PLR has been prepared in 2023 at the mid-point of the CPF period,\nand benefits from updated knowledge about country context, program implementation, and lessons learned.\nIt also suggests forward-looking changes to the results framework, implementation, and risk management.\nThe PLR will inform the engagement with the new government to be elected in June 2024, the Completion\nand Learning Review (CLR) in FY25, and a new CPF planned for FY26.\n3. Immediately after CPF discussion, global and domestic crises hit Mexico, shifting demand for World\nBank collaboration, and affecting CPF implementation and graduation prospects. The COVID-19 pandemic\nresulted in a dramatic economic contraction of 8 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 2020,2\ncompounded by a global recession and the economic fallout from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Although\nMexico continued to access external capital markets on reasonable terms, crisis management altered\npriorities and affected reforms. This undermined CPF implementation and Mexico’s graduation from the\nInternational Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD).3 A shift in client demand for World Bank\nsupport led to a large increase in countercyclical IBRD policy financing versus the previous CPF period at the\nexpense of a fall in demand for investment lending. Several Investment Policy Financing (IPF) operations were\ncanceled or restructured at client request. The World Bank’s analytical engagement helped maintain\ncollaboration through several high-impact reports, which supported the policy content of the Development\nPolicy Financing (DPF) program. Nevertheless, as a result of these two fundamental global and domestic\nshifts, out of the 24 CPF objective indicators, eight have been achieved, one partially achieved, five are on\ntrack, and ten are off track, five of which are unlikely to be achieved.4\n4. This PLR confirms the original strategic direction and the duration of the 2020 CPF but proposes\nadjustments to its objectives and results framework in light of these dual shifts. The PLR confirms the three\nCPF Focus Areas5 but reduces the number of objectives from seven to six. The changes to the results\nframework reflect current reform space, client demand, and implementation capacity. The PLR also raises\nthe overall risk rating from “Moderate” to “Substantial.” The adjustments proposed in the PLR are aligned\nwith World Bank reforms currently under discussion, notably the Evolution Roadmap, which includes an\nelevated strategic role for middle-income countries on the global challenges agenda.6 The PLR thus\nsummarizes what the World Bank is doing in selected global challenges, particularly those addressed more\ndirectly in Focus Area C (Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation; Energy Access; and Water Security and\nAccess) and identifies further opportunities for one World Bank Group (WBG) collaboration, through\ncoordination and deployment of collective knowledge and complementary instruments for greater impact.\n1 Country Partnership Framework, World Bank Report No. 137429-MX.\n2 National Statistics Institute (INEGI)’s monthly employment survey (ENOE) by July 2020.\n3 During preparation, the Graduation Discussion Income (GDI) provided a strong filter for the selection of the activities in the CPF.\n4 These terms are defined in Section III. Summary of Program Implementation and Annex 3.\n5 World Bank, “Mexico Systematic Country Diagnostic,” August 2019.\n6 World Bank, “Evolving the World Bank Group’s Mission, Operations, and Resources: A Roadmap,” December 2022, “Ending Poverty\non a Livable Planet: Report to Governors on World Bank Evolution,” September 2023, including the eight global challenges: (i) Climate\nChange Adaptation and Mitigation; (ii) Fragility and Conflict; (iii) Pandemic Prevention and Preparedness; (iv) Energy Access; (v) Food\nand Nutrition Security; (vi) Water Security and Access; (vii) Enabling Digitalization; and (viii) Protecting Biodiversity and Nature.\n1\n\nII. MAIN CHANGES IN COUNTRY CONTEXT\n5. The CPF was prepared shortly after the current administration assumed power and is aligned with\nthe National Development Plan. President Andrés Manuel López Obrador assumed power in December 2018\nand CPF preparation was completed in 2019. The government consolidated its support in the mid-term\nelections held in June 2021 and local elections in June 2023. Ahead of the next presidential elections in June\n2024, the World Bank is preparing its transition engagement,7 which the PLR will inform.\n6. Immediately after the CPF discussion in 2020, the global COVID-19 pandemic hit. Latin America and\nthe Caribbean (LAC) was the hardest hit region of the world in both health and economic terms. In Mexico,\nthe pandemic resulted in 600,000 estimated excess deaths in 2020, followed by about 800,000 in 2021.8 In\n2020, output suffered its largest collapse since the 1930s. This contraction was driven by social distancing\nmeasures, supply chain disruptions, and risk aversion on the part of consumers and tourists.9 Labor poverty\nincreased from 39.0 percent at end-2019 to 46.0 percent in the same quarter of 2020 (a historical peak due\nto the pandemic), falling back to 37.3 percent by third quarter of 2023. Monetary poverty rates (using the\nofficial poverty line - línea de pobreza por ingresos) showed a similar inverted-U trend going from 49.9\npercent in 2018 to 52.8 in 2020 followed by a rapid decline to 43.5 in 2020.10\n7. Other structural challenges persist. There are significant disparities across states and population\ngroups in Mexico,11 including gender, ethnicity and migration disparities. 12 Income inequality is high. Mexico\nhas a higher Gini coefficient than countries with similar GDP/head13 but the Gini coefficient for household\nincome has declined from 48.6 to 43.1 between 2016 and 2022 due to solid household income growth among\npoorer households. The digital divide risks further entrenching historical disparities in economic\nopportunity.14 Increased violence and insecurity driven by organized crime activities has deterred\ninvestment, reducing the scope to further address economic disparities.15\n8. The government focused on ensuring a solid macroeconomic framework during the pandemic. The\nadministration re-prioritized expenditures to focus on universal cash transfers to the elderly and public\ninvestment in hallmark infrastructure projects. Total public expenditure, at around 27 percent of GDP in 2020,\nexceeded pre-pandemic levels. This was funded by trust funds and tax settlements with large companies.\nThe government now renews its focus on several flagship investments, including (i) the reform of the National\nGuard, (ii) the interoceanic logistic corridor of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, (iii) full operation of the Dos Bocas\nrefinery and progress on energy self-sufficiency, and (iv) labor market reforms.16\n9. GDP has recovered to pre-pandemic levels and the macroeconomic framework remains stable.\nMexico’s potential growth remains subdued on account of low productivity growth and tamed investment.17\nFollowing a mild recession in 2019, the economic contraction accelerated in 2020 with the pandemic-induced\n7 Mexico Electoral and Transition Engagement Advisory Services and Analytics (ASA) (P501990).\n8 Palacio-Mejía, L. “Leading causes of excess mortality in Mexico during the COVID-19 pandemic 2020-2021,” The Lancet, June 2022.\n9 The size of the sector as a share of GDP decreased from 8.6 percent in 2019 to an estimated 6.8 percent in 2020.\n10 CONEVAL: https://www.coneval.org.mx/Medicion/Paginas/ITLP-IS_pobreza_laboral.aspx and\nhttps://www.coneval.org.mx/Medicion/MP/Paginas/Pobreza_2022.aspx.\n11 In 2016, for instance, the average GDP per capita of one of the richest states (Nuevo León) was close to the average in Poland,\nwhile that of the poorest state (Chiapas) was similar to that of Honduras.\n12 World Bank, Macro and Poverty Outlook, fall 2023 http://macropovertyoutlook.worldbank.org. Source :\nhttps://www.hertie-school.org/en/news/detail/content/covid-19-widens-the-digital-divide-in-mexico.\n15 Cervantes, A. et al., “Estimating the economic impact of interpersonal violence in Mexico in 2021: projecting three hypothetical\nscenarios for 2030”, Pan American Journal of Public Health”, March 2023, https://doi.org/10.26633/RPSP.2023.39.\n16 For instance, the substantial increment in the minimum wage, accumulating more than 100 percent increment between 2019 and\n2023 and the outsourcing labor reform, limiting the outsourcing of workers and enhancing formalization of workers.\n17 Investment has been subdued for more than a decade. By 2022, gross fixed capital formation was similar to that of 2012.\n2\n\nrecession. Economic activity returned to its pre-pandemic level in 2022, as GDP grew by 5.7 percent in 2021\nand 3.9 percent in 2022. Growth momentum has continued in 2023, with GDP growing by 3.2 percent year-\non-year.\n10. Smaller firms were most impacted during the pandemic.18 Gross private investment, which had\nstagnated for more than a decade, fell by 4.4 percent and 17.3 percent in real terms in 2019 and 2020,\nrespectively. It rebounded by 9.7 percent in 2021 and by 7.7 percent in 2022. Micro, small, and medium\nenterprises (MSMEs), which in 2019 represented over 99 percent of firms (and about 70 percent of\nemployment and 50 percent of value added), were less resilient during the pandemic, mainly due to their\nlower use of technology to maintain operations.19 Between mid-2019 and mid-2021, Mexico experienced a\nnet loss of about 400,000 MSMEs (1.6 million closures versus 1.2 million new firms). The decline in private\ninvestment during the pandemic was partially offset by higher public infrastructure investment in flagship\nprojects. Recent policy changes in the United States, 20 Mexico’s largest trading partner, have created a boom\nin nearshoring opportunities driven by manufacturing and industrial real estate. 21 During the first three\nquarters of 2023, investment has increased 19.7 percent, surpassing pre-pandemic levels, which could\ncatalyze investment and economic growth, especially in the north and central parts of Mexico.22\n11. Human development outcomes are still suffering from the impact of the pandemic. Mexico\nexperienced one of the highest levels of pandemic-related extraordinary deaths in the world, and among the\nlongest school closures in the region, resulting in about two years of learning losses on average.23 Transfer\nprograms did not significantly offset the effects on household incomes. Between 2016 and 2022, household\nincome from social protection programs (including pensions, scholarships, and other public transfers)\nincreased by 27.3 percent.24 Sweeping reforms to social protection, labor, health, and education programs\nhad only been partially completed by 2020, which led to gaps in coverage, particularly in social protection\nand health.25 Policy shifts, institutional challenges, and turnover in government also aggravated the\npandemic’s impact on inequality of access, opportunity, and outcomes in human development.26\n12. As Mexico has exited the pandemic crisis, the urgency of addressing global challenges has\nincreased, particularly climate change adaptation and mitigation, energy access, and water security and\naccess. Mexico is the second-largest greenhouse gas (GHG) emitter in the region, and among the top ten\nglobal emitters of methane.27 The effects of climate change via both extreme and slow-onset events have\nbeen increasingly felt, with higher disaster-related costs and greater human impact, particularly on the\npoorest.28 Mexican agriculture, tourism, water infrastructure, and transportation have all been increasingly\nhit by climate effects. Current patterns of urbanization, agricultural competition for water resources,\ndeforestation, and the weight of fossil fuel in the energy matrix all make meeting Mexico’s Nationally\nDetermined Contributions (NDC) harder, underscoring the need to advance further on key global challenges.\nTo this end, SHCP has focused on boosting sustainable finance, such as the sustainable taxonomy.\n18 World Bank, “Las Empresas Mexicanas durante la Pandemia de COVID-19,” June 2021.\n19 World Bank, “Unmasking the Impact of COVID-19 on Businesses: Firm Level Evidence from across the World,” 2020.\n20 CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act.\n21 Foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows due to nearshoring could double in the next decade and domestic private investment will\ncomplement the supply chains of exporting industries and enabling sectors.\n22 Oxford Economics, “Mexico Nearshoring,” June 2023.\n23 Mexico registered the highest avoidable mortality rate of all member countries of the OECD, with a rate of 665 per 100,000\ninhabitants.www.eleconomista.com.mx/politica/Mexico-con-la-tasa-de-mortalidad-mas-alta-de-la-OCDE-202311160007.html\n24 INEGI (2023) Comunicado de prensa Núm. 420/23, page 2.\n25 Social assistance coverage in 2020 was similar to 2018, but lower for the poorest quintile. SUMMARY OF PROGRAM IMPLEMENTATION\nProgram and Portfolio Performance\n13. World Bank lending to Mexico has increased, driven by high growth in policy lending. IBRD lending\nhas increased by more than 25 percent in this CPF period relative to the previous one (FY14-19), propelled\nby an eightfold increase in DPF net commitments. At the end of FY23, total approved lending during the CPF\nperiod was US$4.3 billion (US$3.9 billion in DPF), versus US$3.4 billion during the previous CPF (US$0.5 billion\nin DPF). One additional DPF is planned for FY24. IFC’s commitments increased from US$1.62 billion in FY14-\n17 to US$1.75 billion in FY20-23. Annex 5 provides an overview of portfolio performance.\n14. Higher demand for policy lending and reduced appetite for investment lending can be traced to a\ncombination of global challenges and domestic policy shifts. Multiple global crises made fast-disbursing DPF\noperations the instrument of choice. Domestically, policy priorities were focused on a few large public\ninvestment projects, limiting space in the federal budget for other CPF focus areas. The government also\nwithdrew earlier requests for World Bank support in several areas, indicating shifting priorities or views of\nthe benefits of external project financing. Changing policy directions, institutional challenges, high turnover\nin key institutions, and security obstacles further affected policy continuity, implementation, and results.\nWith the 2024 electoral transition approaching, the window of opportunity for new policy reforms and the\npreparation of any further IPF pipeline is now limited.29\n15. The World Bank showed flexibility and pragmatism to deliver results through two main\nengagement strategies. First, IBRD responded to changing policy priorities by focusing on policy lending\nduring COVID-19 while continuing to invest in selected shared priorities: forestry preservation, financial\ninclusion, an improved business environment, and gender equality. IFC introduced upstream pre-investment\nprograms to support market creation and project structuring from an early stage, complemented by advisory\nprojects on climate, gender, and digitalization. Second, at client request, several investment operations were\nrestructured by the Bank, with cancellations of US$894 million out of US$1.28 billion in net commitments.\n16. The World Bank has maintained a strong analytical program to inform DPFs, to add value where\nmore intensive financial engagement was not possible, and to explore new entry-points. Demand-driven\nAdvisory Services and Analytics (ASA) informed key issues across the CPF objectives and maintained World\nBank engagement in many areas in the absence of lending (e.g., education, labor market policy, climate\nchange). The Reimbursable Advisory Services (RAS) instrument – a powerful instrument for middle-income\ncountries like Mexico – has been deployed in the transport sector, with a new agreement signed in July 2023.\n17. The CPF’s intended subnational focus on Mexico’s southern states was advanced through policy\nlending and advisory services. The CPF aimed for a greater impact on Mexico’s southern states, where a\nlarge share of the poorest population lives. This objective was affected by the reduced IPF program to\nchannel further resources to the poorest states in the south, as legal and institutional obstacles prevent direct\nlending to subnational government in Mexico. Still, IBRD supported federal policies (through policy-based\nlending) that generated benefits for the whole country, but had positive effects for lagging states (e.g., the\nUrban Upgrading Program supported under the Environmental Sustainability and Urban Resilience DPF\ntargeted marginalized urban areas with above-average deficits in access to public services and infrastructure\nin southern states). Analytical and advisory engagements have allowed demand-driven support to states, for\nexample through just-in-time support in several sectors (e.g., productivity, education, disaster risk\nmanagement), helping identify new partners and pave the way for potential future engagements (Annex 5).\n18. Fiduciary management has been satisfactory. Financial management and procurement\narrangements for IBRD projects are adequate. IBRD has strengthened client procurement capacity and\n29 The choice of lending instrument also relates to the characteristics of the investment project financing (IPF) instrument, particularly\nits disbursement profile, associated commitment fees and implementation modalities.\n4\n\nharmonized procurement documents are being updated.30 IBRD has also supported higher quality financial\nmanagement at national and project levels, in coordination with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)\nand the national organized accounting profession. Audits are generally on time and unqualified. More\ncustomized, agile approaches, including greater use of digital technologies, will be explored.\n19. The portfolio complied with safeguard policies and the Environmental and Social Framework (ESF).\nProject environmental and social risk ratings have ranged from moderate to low. Targeted supervision and\ncapacity-strengthening for all IPF projects have advanced ESF implementation, including in good practices\nsuch as the Dedicated Grant Mechanism for Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities Project.\n20. IFC’s committed portfolio in Mexico stands at US$2.4 billion, leveraging further private-sector\nfinance. As of December 31st, 2023, IFC portfolio included US$827 million of mobilized resources, the fourth\nlargest portfolio regionally and 13th globally. From FY20 to February 2024, IFC has committed US$2.3 billion\nof long-term financing (including US$900 million of mobilized resources) and US$706 million of short-term\nfinancing.\n21. MIGA’s guarantees in Mexico stand at US$2.3 billion, de-risking foreign investments and lending,\nwhich could lead the way to structure more operations with the financial sector. Mexico is MIGA’s largest\nexposure in the LAC region and globally. As of end-FY23, MIGA’s exposure in Mexico was in support of one\nproject in the energy sector. During the CPF, MIGA has provided guarantees to the Federal Electricity\nCommission to rehabilitate and modernize hydropower plants and to the export credit agency Bancomext to\nhelp exporting firms mitigate the impacts of the pandemic, the latter cancelled in April 2023. In October 2023,\nMIGA issued capital optimization guarantees of $1.9 billion to HSBC, covering the risk of expropriation of\nfunds for the mandatory reserves that HSBC Mexico holds at the central bank of Mexico.\nProgress Towards CPF Objectives\n22. Despite progress, many CPF targets are not on track. The global and domestic shifts described above\nhave both affected CPF implementation and results. Of 24 objective indicators, (i) eight have been achieved,\n(ii) one is partially achieved, (iii) five are on track but require adjustments to be achieved, and (iv) ten are off\ntrack, five of which are unlikely to be achieved as a result of cancellations or restructurings.31 In some areas,\nprogress has been made through other channels, e.g., DPF or ASA as opposed to IPF (see Annexes 3 and 5).\nFocus Area A: Supporting more rapid, more inclusive growth.\n23. In Focus Area A, of six indicators, one is achieved, one is partially achieved, one is on track, and\nthree are off track. Challenges are mainly due to cancellations and restructurings of operations, pandemic\nimpact, and monetary tightening to contain inflation.\n24. Financial intermediation and inclusion results are mixed. Progress on expanding access to credit for\nMSMEs was constrained by the pandemic, as well as liquidity and solvency issues faced by non-banking\nfinancial institutions (Indicator 1.2: MSMEs loans extended). Additional IBRD financing of the “Expanding\nRural Finance Project” was ruled out by debt ceilings during the pandemic and a shift in policy and lending\npriorities (Indicator 1.1: rural microenterprises and SMEs with access to credit). Financial inclusion has been\nexpanded through electronic payments via the new electronic payment platform (Indicator 1.3).\n25. IBRD has supported subnational competition regulation in the telecom, transport, and retail\nsectors. Forty-one subnational laws and regulations were changed to introduce a more competitive\nregulatory framework, achieving Indicator 2.1 (pro-competitive regulatory framework at the subnational\n30 Seven IPFs, including four trust funds are implementing the procurement regulations, taking into account the benefits of their\nflexibilities according to the context, risk, value, and complexity of each project, supported by its own project procurement strategy.\n31 Achieved: the targets were met on time or ahead of time; Partially achieved: half of the targets or less were met and the indicator\nis dropped in the PLR; On track: more than half of the targets have been met; Off track: half of the targets or less have been met.\n5\n\nlevel). IBRD also supported the conceptualization and design of the national digital platform aimed at\nenhancing business regulation across the regulatory governance cycle. IFC support to Altan Redes (the\ncompany responsible for the shared network) contributed to an increase in the population covered by\nwireless broadband to 70 percent as of January 2022 (Indicator 2.2). A strong ASA program on inclusive growth included the 2022\nProductivity Report and joint IBRD-IFC work on nearshoring, entrepreneurship, and eco-industrial parks.\nFocus Area B: Strengthening institutions for public finance, service delivery, and economic inclusion.\n26. In Focus Area B, of nine indicators, three have been achieved, one is on track, and five are off track.\nOn public service delivery, under Objective 3 (enhance the management of public resources), no progress\nwas made on Indicator 3.1 (population captured by the single identification system) due to the client decision\nto cancel the “National Digital Identity System Project” in 2022, reflecting priority changes. Support to public\nfinance through the “Modernization of Public Financial Management Systems in Mexico Project” was\nconstrained by the pandemic and implementation delays, which limited progress on Indicators 3.2 (budget\nexecuted through the Integrated Financial Management Information System) and 3.3 (time to produce\nconsolidated budget execution information). The project was restructured and is now in problem project\nstatus. IFC’s support to Public Private Partnership (PPP) transactions included two projects successfully\nawarded in May 2021 under the Los Cabos Water Advisory Project (Indicator 3.4: PPP transactions).\n27. Despite the impact of the pandemic, specific results indicators in education and social protection\nservice delivery are encouraging. Objective 4 (strengthen institutional capacity to deliver inclusive social\nservices) has been supported through the national early childhood development strategy (indicator 4.1\nadoption at the state level). Indicator 4.2 (pilots of the new integrated health networks at the state level) was\nnot achieved due to changes in government priorities. IBRD technical assistance was provided to the National\nInstitute of Public Health and the Secretariat of Finance and Public Credit (SHCP). Almost 52,000 additional\npatients were attended between 2018 and 2022 by IFC supported healthcare services, exceeding the targets\nfor Indicator 4.3 (patients benefiting from the healthcare services). Objective 5 (strengthen the capacity of\nthe social protection system for economic inclusion) was achieved through the “Social Protection System\nProject” and support to Mexico’s National Employment Service (SNE). Indicator 5.1 (Integrated Social\nProtection Centers established) was surpassed. Indicator 5.2 (implementation of modernized processes at\nSNE) has also been achieved through support to SNE, including the expansion of its office network.\nFocus Area C: Enabling sustainable infrastructure and climate action.\n28. In Focus Area C four of the nine objective indicators have been achieved; three are on track (after\nsome adjustments); and two are off track. Notable results have been achieved on housing and sustainable\nlandscape management, despite some implementation delays and restructuring.\n29. Progress has been lower than expected under Objective 6 on more inclusive and sustainable\ninfrastructure services. The “Water Security and Resilience of the Valley of Mexico Project” (PROSEGHIR),\napproved in February 2020, was delayed for over two years, slowing progress on Indicator 6.2 (people with\nimproved water supply reliability), but remains a priority in line with the Evolution Roadmap’s global\nchallenge on water security and access. A project to support Mexico’s National Infrastructure Fund\n(FONADIN) was dropped during preparation, affecting Indicator 6.1 (private capital mobilization for\ninfrastructure). Nevertheless, almost US$570 million have been mobilized by the issuance of sustainable\nbonds with a gender perspective by the infrastructure development bank, BANOBRAS. Despite US$800\nmillion of IFC additional private finance mobilization and own account investments in infrastructure, results\nare below expectations for indicator 6.1. MIGA’s guarantee played a catalytic role in the Tierra Mojada Power\nPlant project, which was cancelled in December 2020 owing to the successful refinancing of the project’s\n6\n\nbank debt with a bond, issued after the project had become operational. Although minimum power was\ndelivered during MIGA’s contract period, the project has generated 5,828 GWh of electricity above the target\nfor Indicator 6.4 (total power generated). In June 2023, MIGA also signed a guarantee supporting CFE for the\nrehabilitation and modernization of hydropower plants. The “Energy Efficiency in Public Facilities Project”\n(PRESEMEH) was scaled down to one third of the original US$150 million, reducing progress on Indicators 6.3\n(energy savings) and 7.1 (GHG emissions reduced). Indicator 6.5 (access to low-cost resilient housing) was\nreached through the “Improving Access to Affordable Housing Project” and IFC support to a housing provider.\n30. Progress on Objective 7 on climate change mitigation has been satisfactory. Sustainable landscape\nmanagement practices (Indicator 7.2) and the number of beneficiaries, particularly women and indigenous\npeoples, implementing sustainable management schemes (Indicator 7.3) have increased with satisfactory\nimplementation of the “Strengthening Entrepreneurship in Productive Forest Landscapes Project”\n(PROFOEM). Similarly, power generated from renewable energy sources supported by IFC has achieved its\ntarget (Indicator 7.4), with potential for further support. Indicators 7.1 (GHG emissions) and 7.3 (sustainable\nmanagement schemes in rural areas) were affected by restructurings of the forest, sustainable landscapes,\nand energy projects, but remain a priority to help tackle the global challenge of climate change.\nProgress Towards Corporate Commitments\n31. Corporate commitments have been mainstreamed across World Bank operations. The portfolio has\nexceeded corporate and regional targets since FY21 with 100 percent of IBRD projects gender-tagged and all\nactive projects complying with citizen engagement requirements. On climate, IBRD reached an average of\n41.3 percent of co-benefits in FY21-23, and IFC and MIGA had an average of 54.5 and 44.0 percent\nrespectively of new projects and guarantees tagged as climate-related since FY20 (Annex 6).\nPartnerships and Leveraging\n32. The World Bank has deepened coordination with other development partners. Under the\n“Environment Sustainability and Urban Resilience DPF” prior actions on climate, forests, and environmental\nmanagement were coordinated with partners (Annex 5). The Partnership for Market Implementation, a\nmulti-donor initiative led by the World Bank,32 has provided technical assistance on carbon pricing. The\nUnited Kingdom, the United States, and IBRD have joined forces to support Mexico’s forestry program\n(Objective 7). For the remainder of the CPF, closer collaboration within the WBG and with the IDB is expected,\nincluding on selected global challenges and private capital mobilization.\nIV. EMERGING LESSONS\n33. CPF design needs to adjust to the policy framework and operating environment, taking a\npragmatic, flexible, and creative approach to opportunities and risks. A realistic assessment of country\ncontext – policy priorities, financing constraints, political economy, and implementation capacity and\nlikelihood – is crucial. While the pandemic was impossible to predict, other governance, institutional, and\nsectoral risks could have been assessed more realistically and the program designed accordingly. The PLR\nbuilds on these lessons, with greater program selectivity and a more realistic risk assessment, seeking\nopportunities and balancing what is desirable with what is politically and technically possible at the federal,\nsubnational and sector levels. The Evolution Roadmap, with an enhanced value proposition for middle-\nincome countries, opens opportunities for a more integrated one World Bank Group approach at the project\nlevel and in joint knowledge engagements, such as on nearshoring, climate finance, financial inclusion, digital,\nenergy supply reliability and water. Global knowledge initiatives (e.g., the World Development Report on\nmigration) under the new Knowledge Compact may open doors to new forms of collaboration.\n34. Policy-lending can provide rapid support in response to crises, helping finance public expenditures\n32 Among them the European Commission, Germany, Spain, Sweden, Japan, United Kingdom, United States, and Australia.\n7\n\nand laying the foundations for a resilient recovery, while fostering innovations. In recent decades, Mexico\nhas followed a pattern of countercyclical lending, increasing exposure in downturns and crises (e.g., new\ncommitments of US$10.5 billion in FY08-10 and US$3.6 billion FY20-22). During COVID-19, three of four DPFs\napproved in FY20-22 directly supported pandemic crisis response and recovery, including the first “Build Back\nBetter” DPF. DPFs also supported innovative policy reforms (e.g., fintech, gender, and sustainable finance).\n35. IPF preparation can be challenging and fragile, yet investment lending operations have usually led\nto positive outcomes when implemented. Despite an investment pipeline reflecting the strength of the\ndialogue in many sectors, the government made a series of decisions not to proceed with many IPF\noperations. Complex project design, including inter- and intra-institutional coordination challenges,\nimplementation delays, partial cancellations, have jeopardized impact. Of the five IPF projects that closed in\nFY20-23, three were found satisfactory by the IEG (e.g., simple project design and client ownership\ncontributed to successful implementation). Four additional IPF projects are rated moderately satisfactory or\nbetter and are expected to achieve their objectives by closing in FY25. Reduced appetite for IPF and\nrestrictions on the use of this and other instruments (e.g., PforR) call for a close dialogue on design features,\nimplementation challenges, lessons learned to develop a new federal and potential also subnational pipeline.\n36. Analytical work has added technical value to policy making and served as a technical foundation\nfor policy lending. In the absence of new investment lending, the ASA program has positioned the World\nBank as a trusted adviser on evidence-based policy reforms, strengthening DPF design. Expansion of financial\naccess in Mexico was supported through the Financial Inclusion DPF, the COVID-19 Financial Access DPF, and\nthe Promoting Women’s Economic Opportunities and Sustainable Productivity Growth DPF. These operations\nbuilt on the 2016 and 2022 Financial Sector Assessment Programs, the Financial Inclusion Global Initiative,\nthe Gender Report, and IFC support on business regulations and SME access to credit.\n37. For IFC, deepening the relationship with the Ministry of Finance, diversifying business\ndevelopment efforts across industries and client types, while also emphasizing non-financial benefits, is\nexpected to both mitigate sector concentration risk and strengthen IFC’s value proposition. IFC investments\nin renewable energy in Mexico have grown substantially, representing almost 100 percent of new IFC\ninfrastructure investments from FY18 to FY20. Subsequent difficulties in the sector created a shock to IFC’s\ninfrastructure target, which was only partially mitigated by increased support for digital infrastructure. IFC’s\ndiversification to new players within the financial system and its use of the highest environmental, social, and\ngovernance standards have enhanced IFC’s contribution to the financial inclusion and climate agenda,\nincluded under CPF focus areas A and C. The latter can be illustrated by IFC investments in the Sustainable\nBond issued by GF Mega, structured under a sustainability framework to promote financial inclusion,\nwomen’s empowerment, and climate-friendly practices; and the Partial Credit Guarantee to IDEI Green Bond\nIssuance, to finance Excellence in Design for Greater Efficiencies (EDGE)-certified green residential projects.\nSynergies and complementarities among IFC, IBRD, and MIGA can also strengthen product and market\ndiversification.\nV. ADJUSTMENTS TO COUNTRY PARTNERSHIP FRAMEWORK\n38. This PLR confirms the strategic direction and the duration of the CPF but proposes adjustments to\nthe results framework. The PLR confirms that the three CPF Focus Areas remain appropriate to address\nMexico’s structural growth, inclusion, and sustainability challenges identified in the Systematic Country\nDiagnostic.33 The PLR adjusts Objective 2 to reflect new engagements with the private sector and drops\nObjective 3 to reflect implementation delays and cancellations. Objective 2 includes new indicators on the\nadoption of a framework to certify industrial parks. Focus Area 3 will continue supporting Mexico in some of\nthe most pressing global challenges, e.g., Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation; Energy Access; and\nWater Security and Access. The results matrix has been streamlined to reflect reform space, client demand,\n33 World Bank, “Mexico Systematic Country Diagnostic,” August 2019.\n8\n\nand implementation capacity by sector34 (Annex 2).\nFocus Area A: Supporting more rapid, more inclusive growth.\n39. The PLR maintains Objective 1 to “foster financial intermediation and inclusion” and continues\nsupporting sustainable finance. With limited space for new lending, the PLR proposes to support Mexico’s\nsustainable finance agenda through analytical support, including the development of a biodiversity taxonomy\nand associated regulations, building on the joint IFC-IBRD 30x30 Zero advisory services, which also aims to\nraise the share of green assets in bank portfolios. On financial intermediation, new objectives have been\nadded on increasing account ownership and reducing the gender gap in digital payments. Indicators on users\nand payments through the digital payments’ platform and MSME loans have been revised to reflect progress.\n40. Objective 2 is adjusted from aiming to “reduce regulatory and competition barriers to economic\ngrowth” to “support private sector investment.” IBRD will support ASA on the subnational implementation\nof a national digital platform to improve business regulation. Based on analytical work on productivity,\nentrepreneurship, and eco-industrial parks, IBRD and IFC will support FDI attraction for the piloting of eco-\nindustrial parks. The PLR includes two new indicators on a framework to certify industrial parks including\nenvironmental sustainability and the number of IFC transactions tagged as “nearshoring.”\nFocus Area B: Strengthening institutions for service delivery and inclusion.\n41. Focus Area B is adjusted from “Strengthening institutions for public finance, service delivery, and\neconomic inclusion” to “Strengthening institutions for service delivery and inclusion.” The PLR drops\nObjective 3 to “enhance the management of public resources” due to project implementation delays and\ncancellations. IBRD will continue supporting SHCP plans to strengthen human resource and public investment\nmanagement and its integration with the budget system as well as the implementation of Mexico’s\nsustainable finance strategy. IFC will continue structuring and financing PPP projects in key sectors, yet with\nmore limited scope, given reduced federal funding to structure projects and uneven subnational capacities.\n42. Objective 4 (new Objective 3) is revised to “strengthen the capacity to deliver inclusive education\nand health services.” IBRD will remain engaged in early childhood education and support the recovery of\nlearning losses by (i) improving teaching practices; (ii) developing early warning systems to identify students\nat risk of dropping out and targeted efforts to lower this risk; and (iii) catalyzing human capital formation by\nexpanding early childhood care and education services. IFC will continue to support innovative, scalable\nmodels for high-quality, affordable private health-care services. In line with the pandemic prevention and\npreparedness global challenge, IBRD has shifted its engagement to formulating proposals to enhance\nreadiness and responses for health crises and the resilience of health financing to population ageing.\n43. Objective 5 (new Objective 4) is adjusted to “strengthen the capacity to deliver inclusive social\nservices.” IBRD work with SNE to use good practices and digital tools to support social protection and\nimprove the integration of vulnerable members of the labor force (e.g., women, youth, and migrants).\nFocus Area C: Enabling sustainable infrastructure and climate action.\n44. Objective 6 (new Objective 5) on more inclusive and sustainable infrastructure services remains a\npriority, despite challenges in infrastructure sectors. In the water sector, IBRD will continue to support water\nsupply and sanitation activities through its operation in the Valley of Mexico and potential investments and\nadvisory work in the northern part of the country (e.g., wastewater treatment and reuse, groundwater\nmonitoring and management, and irrigation modernization) in line with the water security and access global\nchallenge. The energy efficiency project (PRESEMEH) will be closed. MIGA will expand its presence through\nits guarantee to CFE supporting efforts towards tackling the global challenge on energy efficiency and access.\nIBRD will support Mexico’s development banks on private sector capital mobilization, especially for\n34 The PLR drops nine, adjusts thirteen, and reconfirms two out of 24 objective indicators, and adds five new indicators.\n9\n\ninfrastructure and energy. IFC will support competitive private energy markets and digital infrastructure,\nfocusing on renewables and telecom, in addition to other areas where private investment can help meeting\nthe growing needs from nearshoring. WBG collaboration with financial entities and funds will be\nstrengthened to promote private capital mobilization to address infrastructure needs in key sectors such as\ntransport, energy, water, and real estate. Indicators have been adjusted to reflect progress and challenges.\n45. The World Bank will intensify efforts to support Mexico’s climate change goals under Objective 7\n(new Objective 6). Cross-sectoral climate change mitigation and adaptation, one of the key global challenges\noutlined in the Evolution Roadmap, will be supported through ASA. IFC will mobilize knowledge and\ninvestments targeted at financial institutions, fintech, and funds to develop sound climate portfolios. MIGA\nwill seek opportunities to support renewable energy projects. MIGA has also issued new capital optimization\nguarantees to HSBC covering the risk of expropriation of funds for the mandatory reserves that HSBC Mexico\nholds at the central bank of Mexico. The benefits of the MIGA-enabled capital relief will provide financing of\nUS$1.5 billion to climate finance sub-projects over 2023-2026. IBRD operations on forestry and agriculture\nwill continue with a focus on forest-dependent communities and on strengthening community and producer\norganizations in the management and entrepreneurship of productive landscapes, protecting biodiversity\nand nature as a key global challenge. The World Bank will seek innovation in financial solutions for disaster\nmanagement and climate resilience and support the sustainable taxonomy. Objectives have been adjusted.\nVI. Program Implementation\nProgram and Portfolio Performance\n1. World Bank lending to Mexico has increased. As of December 2023, the World Bank active\nportfolio includes US$1.68 billion from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development\n(IBRD), US$2.4 billion committed portfolio from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), and US$536\nmillion from the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA). Under the current CPF, the total\nIBRD lending approved sums up to US$4.3 billion (US$1.1 billion average per year) relative to US$560.0\nmillion in the previous CPF. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) also committed investments\nincreased in the first four years relative to the same period of the previous CPF, from US$1.62 billion\nduring FY14-17 to US$1.75 billion during FY20-23. Responding to global context and increased client\nappetite for countercyclical financing sources, DPF increased to US$3.9 billion compared to US$0.5 billion\nunder the previous CPF.228 Over FY20-FY23, four Development Policy Financing (DPF) operations were\nextended to the Mexican authorities, three directly supporting the COVID-19 crisis response and\nrecovery, including IBRD’s first Build Back Better DPF. For FY24, the pipeline for the remaining CPF\nconsists of only one DPF project. In addition, IBRD has an active Bank-executed trust fund portfolio\nbenefiting the country which comprises 34 trust funds for a total net commitment of US$71.1 million.\n2. IBRD portfolio has moved from an average of sixteen projects during the previous CPF to ten\nprojects during the current CPF, with a gradual reduction of investment project financing (IPF). IPF was\nreduced from 11 projects in 2020 to 7 in 2023. The active IBRD portfolio as of December 2023, comprises\nfive IBRD loans (US$1.6 billion), complemented by two Global Environment Facility (GEF) projects, and\none recipient executed trust-funded project. Since the CPF was discussed by the Board, seven IBRD\nprojects and one GEF stand-alone project have been approved. World Bank Business Intelligence Reporting, Standard Reports, and Analysis for Office.\n4. A strong analytical program helped maintain the dialogue and explore entry-points for further\ncollaboration with the current and the next administration. Formal Advisory Services and Analytics (ASA),\nsuch as the Female Labor Force Participation Report,229 the Pensions Policy Support Program, and the\nProductivity Report,230 helped to set up the agenda, informing reform options and lending, such as in the\n“Promoting Women Economic Opportunities and Sustainable Productivity Growth DPF” operation. Just-\nin-time support, such as for the education, health, social protection and labor sectors, helped maintain\nthe dialogue and pave the ground for future engagements (e.g., an assessment of learning lost during\nschool closures). IBRD has become a key partner in assisting the authorities implement a comprehensive\nearly childhood education and development strategy; IBRD’s analytical support has been welcomed by\nthe Secretariat of Finance and Public Credit (SHCP) and health sector agencies to assess the sustainability\nand resilience of health financing in the face of shocks and population ageing; while Mexico has turned\nrepeatedly to IBRD’s Social Protection and Jobs practice for support on pension reform, modernizing its\nlabor market intermediation services and for support in integrating migrants into the economy. In\naddition, IBRD’s engagement focused strongly on helping the government advance the climate resilience,\nforestry, and land use agendas. As a result, in 2020 an innovative “Environmental Sustainability and Urban\nResilience DPF” was approved, which addressed development challenges around the increase of the\nresilience of the most vulnerable municipalities, the gradual reform towards non-deforestation criteria in\nagriculture support programs, and local air quality provisions to mitigate black carbon. Likewise, this DPF\nalso strongly featured IBRD’s urban engagement. Strong operational engagement in the water sector has\nbeen further supported by analytical work laying the foundation for strengthening IBRD’s engagement in\nthe sector at national and subnational levels. Engagements with the SHCP on disaster risk management,\ne.g., technical assistance to strengthen the risk management strategy related to natural hazard risk at the\nfederal and subnational levels, helped respond to core client demands and laid the foundation for longer-\nterm reforms on the Evolution Roadmap global challenges’ agenda. ASAs also led to demand in trust-funds\nand other concessional funding.\n5. Reimbursable Advisory Services are a powerful engagement instrument for middle-income\ncountries. A Reimbursable Advisory Services (RAS) agreement was signed in transport in June 2023 and\n229 World Bank, “Female Labor Force Participation in Mexico,” March 2021.\n230 World Bank, “Productivity Growth in Mexico: Understanding Main Dynamics and Key Drivers,” January 2022.\n67\n\nother RAS engagements were explored in line with sector demand in the education and health sectors but\ndid not materialize.\n6. Given legal challenges for direct lending to the sub-national level and security risks, IBRD relied\non ASA to support subnational. For example, IBRD has supported the municipalities of Tulum and San\nCristobal de las Casas in developing their Municipal Climate Action Plans, and in March 2023, launched a\ntechnical assistance program (financed by the Climate Investment Facility) to develop a city climate action\nplan for the metropolitan area of Oaxaca, including all the 25 municipalities, located in one of the\ncountry’s poorest states in the south.\n7. Similarly, advisory programs helped to keep a strong involvement from public and private\ninstitutions in priority areas such as climate. Under the 30x30 Zero project in Mexico, for instance,\nIFC/IBRD collaborated with Mexico’s Central Bank (Banxico), originally through the Sustainable Finance\nCommittee, part of the Financial Stability Board, to examine the different aspects of “greening the\nfinancial sector”: (i) Green Taxonomy, (ii) reporting and disclosure, (iii) social and climate risk analysis, and\n(iv) ecoefficiency and decarbonization. A gender agenda with financial institutions and regulators is being\ncarried out jointly by IFC and IBRD to address policy and market challenges to untap and scale new\nopportunities. IFC participated in the four working groups and supported the green Taxonomy, which\nbecame the Sustainable Taxonomy. Also, through the Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) Green\nBuildings program, IFC has supported the public and private sectors’ green agenda, reaching 4.9 million\nsquare meters certified with the Excellence in Design for Greater Efficiencies (EDGE) certificate, and\nthrough the TechEmerge Sustainable Cooling Cities program, the successful closure of 11 pilots by FY23\nwhere participants were able to decide on potential scale-up of innovate cooling solutions either at\nadopter or at broader market. This EDGE achievement positions Mexico as the third country globally with\nthe largest certified floor space. IBRD and IFC are also working together on how to harness nearshoring\ninvestments in Mexico for which a close coordination with the government would be key. Teams are\nworking on a strategy to leverage this opportunity to address development gaps (notably declining\nproductivity, high informality, asymmetric integration into global value chains, and low technological\nupgrade by local firms), while promoting a sustainable and inclusive approach of these investments and\npublic-private coordination to provide the enabling factors. MIGA is also planning to join those strategic\nconversation as one World Bank to explore opportunities to deploy MIGA de-risking solutions to enhance\nbankability of projects, facilitate public-private investments, and the mobilization of foreign capital in\nMexico. More specifically, the close collaboration with IBRD and IFC proved crucial in the development of\nthe Federal Commission Electricity (CFE) project, where MIGA provided non-honoring guarantees to a\nstate-owned utility, given rapidly evolving conditions in the energy sector.\"\n8. Portfolio management has incorporated fiduciary considerations. On procurement, tailored\nproject procurement strategies have been designed in line with each project’s context, risks, regulations,\nand complexities, allowing for flexibility and better execution of Procurement Plans, but also to overcome\nchallenges. These include misalignment of the procurement processes to optimize the use of resources in\ncontracts, and lack of government staff with experience conducting procurement processes financed with\nIBRD resources. Mitigation measures have included additional support to implementing entities, including\nin the use of innovative methods such as the use of rated criteria, and harmonization of procurement\ndocuments with the most recent country’s regulations and policies. Performance on financial\nmanagement continues to be generally satisfactory. Challenges related to budgeting and limited fiscal\nspace for investment operations, including trust funds, remain. IBRD loan proceeds are budgeted only on\nan annual basis, and grant funds cannot be received directly by federal entities, affecting planning and\ncausing implementation delays. Limited federal budgetary resources have also led to a reduction in the\nscope of some investment projects. To tackle these challenges, IBRD has continued to promote fiduciary\n68\n\ncapacity development for project-implementing entities through the provision of regular training (i.e., on\nIBRD’s systematic tracking of exchanges in procurement, STEP) and workshops (i.e., a fiduciary workshop\nheld in June 2023), and through actively engaging with the organized accounting profession in Mexico in\ncoordination with the Inter-American Development Bank.\n9. Safeguards ratings and environment and social (E&S) standards performance ranged between\nmoderately satisfactory and satisfactory, with no projects closed with pending E&S measures. IBRD has\nprovided oversight, supervision, follow-up, and capacity-building support, for all IPF projects. One of the\ninnovations of the Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) is the recognition that climate change is\naffecting the nature and location of IBRD-financed projects. It sets out a vision to support client countries\nto decarbonize and invest in resilience to help overcome climate change as a fundamental threat to\ndevelopment in our lifetime. Although the requirement for new operations, the Paris Alignment\nassessment, is distinct from the E&S assessment set out in the ESF, the ESF’s standards reinforce the World\nBank’s ability to ensure financing aligns with the goals of the Paris Agreement.\n10.      30\n\n−    De 2022 a 2023, el porcentaje de programas sociales con aprobación de indicadores se incrementó\n        en 5 puntos porcentuales, pasando de 73% a 78%. Lo anterior implica que cinco programas lograron\n        obtener el dictamen de Aprobación condicionada en 2023 y tres programas transitaron a Aprobación\n        directa.\n   −    De la totalidad de programas sujetos al proceso de aprobación en 2023, 13 de ellos, equivalentes\n        a 22%, aún tienen pendiente consolidar y afinar el diseño de sus indicadores. Es esencial que estos\n        programas continúen con el acompañamiento técnico y metodológico que brinda el CONEVAL para\n        que, eventualmente, logren obtener un dictamen de aprobación favorable, garantizando así una\n        medición efectiva de sus resultados y una mejora del cumplimiento de sus objetivos.\n   −    De los 13 programas con dictamen que aún no cumple con criterios mínimos, cuatro (31%) son\n        programas prioritarios de la administración actual. Esto subraya la importancia y el desafío continuo\n        de innovar su sistema de medición de resultados y optimizar la entrega de los bienes o servicios\n        que proporcionan. Es esencial destacar que estos cuatro programas cuentan con un presupuesto\n        total de $118,438 millones de pesos, lo que equivale a 14% del presupuesto total destinado a los\n        programas sociales que están en el proceso de aprobación.\n\n\n\nInforme de Enfoque de Resultados 2023\n\nEl informe tiene como objetivo el analizar si las Matrices de Indicadores para Resultados de los programas\nsociales identifican de forma clara y delimitada a una población objetivo y el cambio sustancial que se\nespera en esta; asimismo, si los indicadores del nivel de Propósito miden dichos cambios. Además, valora\nque los bienes y servicios (Componentes) sean necesarios y suficientes para el cumplimiento del objetivo\ncentral del programa.\n\nDurante el 2023, se publicó el Informe de Enfoque de Resultados 202334, entre los resultados se destacan\nlos siguientes hallazgos:\n\n    −    La valoración del EdR de los programas y acciones sociales para 2023 muestra un comportamiento\n         favorable, ya que 57% de programas y acciones cuentan con Orientación a Resultados, 26% deben\n         mejorar la OR y únicamente 17% no presentan una definición clara de su objetivo central.\n    −    En términos de Medición de Resultados, actualmente 45% de los programas logra una medición\n         adecuada de su Propósito, en contraste con 17% que necesita mejorar sus indicadores para reflejar\n         resultados más precisos y 38% que aún carece de indicadores robustos para supervisar su\n         Propósito, lo cual señala una considerable oportunidad para desarrollar indicadores que permitan\n         una medición sólida y precisa del objetivo central de los programas y acciones sociales.\n    −    Con relación a la Asociación Lógica, en 2023 únicamente 40% de los programas y acciones sociales\n         muestran una AL adecuada. No obstante, 42% de los programas todavía requiere fortalecer su AL,\n         y 17% no muestra una AL adecuada, lo que apunta a áreas significativas de mejora.\nAnálisis de vinculación entre la Matriz de Indicadores para Resultados y las Reglas de Operación\n2023\n\nEl análisis de vinculación entre la MIR y las ROP de los programas sociales de modalidad presupuestaria\n“S”, analiza la consistencia entre el diseño, seguimiento y operación del programa social, de esta forma se\n\n34 El análisis se puede consultar en el siguiente enlace:\nhttps://www.coneval.org.mx/coordinacion/Documents/monitoreo/informes/Informe_EdR_2023.pdf\n                                                               31\n\nconoce si el programa identifica con claridad y de forma delimitada, en su MIR y ROP, la problemática\npública y la población objetivo, además de los bienes y servicios que entrega a dicha población. Lo anterior,\notorga certeza sobre los objetivos que pretenden lograr los programas sociales y permite llevar a cabo un\nadecuado monitoreo y evaluación de su desempeño para contribuir a la transparencia y rendición de\ncuentas.\n\nEn de 2023 se elaboró el análisis y se presentaron los resultados a la Comisión Ejecutiva, posteriormente\nse elaboró el informe y se publicó35. A continuación, se presenta un resumen del análisis:\n\n  −    Del análisis se derivan tres niveles de vinculación (Adecuado, Moderado y Deficiente), los cuales\n       ayudan a identificar el tipo de ajuste necesario para lograr una correcta vinculación entre los\n       documentos de diseño, seguimiento y operación del programa social.\n  −    En cuanto a la vinculación del Propósito de la MIR y el objetivo general de las ROP, 30 (67%)\n       programas sociales logran un nivel de vinculación Alto; 10 (22%) un nivel Medio; y 5 (11%) un nivel\n       Bajo.\n  −    Respecto a la distribución por dependencia, BIENESTAR, Secretaría de Gobernación (SEGOB) y\n       Secretaría del Trabajo y Previsión Social tienen el 100% de sus programas sociales en el nivel de\n       vinculación Alto. En cambio, el Consejo Nacional de Humanidades, Ciencias y Tecnologías\n       (Conahcyt) tiene todos sus programas en el nivel Bajo. Asimismo, Secretaría de Cultura (Cultura), la\n       Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (SEMARNAT) y la Secretaría de Educación\n       Pública (SEP) tienen algunos programas sociales que se sitúan en este último nivel.\n  −    Al analizar los resultados por cada uno de los elementos que conforman la fase 1, se observa que,\n       en promedio, los programas sociales presentan una mayor vinculación respecto al problema público\n       que a la población objetivo.\n  −    En cuanto a la vinculación entre los Componentes de la MIR y los objetivos específicos de las ROP,\n       27 (60%) de los programas sociales alcanzan un nivel de vinculación Alto; 14 (31%) un nivel Medio;\n       y 4 (9%) un nivel Bajo.\n  −    Referente a la distribución por dependencia; BIENESTAR, IMSS-Bienestar, el Instituto Nacional de\n       los Pueblos Indígenas, SEGOB y STPS tienen el 100% de sus programas sociales en el nivel de\n       vinculación Alto. Por el contrario, el Conahcyt tiene todos sus programas en el nivel Medio. Por su\n       parte, Cultura, la Secretaría de Desarrollo Agrario, Territorial y Urbano (SEDATU) y la SEP tienen\n       algunos programas sociales que se sitúan en el nivel Bajo.\n\n\n\nInforme de monitoreo 2023 de los Fondos de Aportaciones Federales del Ramo 33 del ámbito social\n\nEl informe tiene como objetivo el monitorear los Fondos de Aportaciones Federales del Ramo 33 del ámbito\nsocial a través de su presupuesto, los objetivos e indicadores establecidos en la Matriz de Indicadores para\nResultados (MIR) y los proyectos de inversión.\n\nDurante el 2023 se elaboró y publicó36 el Informe de monitoreo 2023 de los Fondos de Aportaciones\nFederales del Ramo 33 del ámbito social en la página del CONEVAL, asimismo se envió a las dependencias\n\n35 El análisis se puede consultar en el siguiente enlace:\nhttps://www.coneval.org.mx/coordinacion/Documents/monitoreo/informes/Analisis_vinculacion_MIR_ROP_2023.pdf\n36 El informe se puede consultar en el siguiente enlace:\nhttps://www.coneval.org.mx/coordinacion/IMPPS/Documents/RAMO33/Informe_2023/Informe_Ramo33_2023.pdf\n                                                               32\n\ny entidades coordinadoras el Informe, así como las Fichas de Enfoque de Resultados y las Fichas de\nmonitoreo. Para avanzar en el\ndesarrollo social de la población más vulnerable, el gobierno actual instrumentó una estrategia que incluye\nponer en marcha programas sociales encaminados a la atención de la mejora educativa, el bienestar social\ny la mejora laboral, cuya población objetivo son personas con discapacidad, población de zonas rurales,\nestudiantes y jóvenes, entre otros. Durante el 2023, se elaboró y publicó el informe.37\n\n\n     ▪    En 2023, el presupuesto para los 16 programas prioritarios existentes asciende a $512,806 millones\n          de pesos, lo que representa un aumento del 20 % en términos reales en comparación con el\n          presupuesto asignado en 2019 para los programas que en ese momento se clasificaban como\n          prioritarios. En 2019, estos programas constituían el 23 % del presupuesto total destinado a\n          programas y acciones sociales, pero para 2023, este porcentaje ha aumentado a poco más del\n          40%.\n     ▪    El análisis de Enfoque de Resultados (EdR) 2023 muestra un panorama alentador. De los\n          programas prioritarios, el 69% (11) posee Orientación a Resultados (OR) en su objetivo principal.\n          Además, el 50% (8) mide efectivamente sus resultados. No obstante, solo el 38% (6) presenta\n          Asociación Lógica (AL) entre sus Componentes y el objetivo principal. Estos hallazgos son\n          relevantes para planificar la Estrategia de Atención de dichos programas el próximo año.\n\n\n\n\nLas Fichas de monitoreo se pueden consultar en el siguiente enlace:\nhttps://www.coneval.org.mx/coordinacion/IMPPS/Paginas/Fichas_Monitoreo_2023.aspx\n37 Se puede consultar en la siguiente dirección electrónica:\nhttps://www.coneval.org.mx/coordinacion/IMPPS/Documents/Programas_acciones_sociales/Programas_Prioritarios/2023/Informe_Programas_Pri\noritarios_2023.pdf\n                                                                 33\n\n▪    De los 16 programas prioritarios, 14 están vinculados a al menos un derecho social; 10 de ellos\n        fomentan el derecho a una alimentación nutritiva y de calidad, y cinco programas cada uno apoyan\n        los derechos a la educación y al trabajo.
